reading.rtitle: How to Read an Abstract in Ninety Seconds
paras: Nobody reads a scientific paper from the first word to the last one, and nobody expects you to. What experienced readers do is read the abstract, decide in about ninety seconds whether the paper is worth an hour of their afternoon, and move on. The abstract is not a summary in the ordinary sense. It is four moves in a fixed order, and once you can see the four, an abstract in any field stops being a wall of text and becomes a form with four boxes. The trick is that each of the four boxes is written in a different kind of English, and if you read all four the same way, all four are harder than they need to be.

The first box is the background, and it is the only part written in the present. Something is known, something is not known, and the gap between the two is why this study exists. Read it for one thing only: the last sentence, which is almost always the aim. The second box is the method, and it is the box that frightens most readers. It should not. It is written almost entirely in the passive, in the past, in short declarative sentences: samples were collected, seedlings were assessed at baseline, the data were analyzed in three independent trials. Nobody is mentioned, because who did it is not the point. The method box has no argument in it at all. It is a recipe with the cook removed.

The third box is the results, and this is where the sentences get short and the numbers arrive. Two words do most of the work here and both are easy to misread. Significant does not mean large or important: in a paper it means unlikely to be the result of chance, and a significant finding can be tiny. And to account for does not mean to explain in the everyday sense: when a paper says that temperature accounted for most of the variation, it means temperature was the cause of most of it. The fourth box is the conclusion, and it is the most cautious English in the whole paper. Authors rarely say that something is true. They conclude that the evidence suggests, that a mechanism may be involved, that one explanation can be ruled out.

Two more things are worth knowing before you go near a database. The first is that peer-reviewed does not mean correct, it means that other specialists in the field read the paper before it was published and did not find a reason to stop it. That is a real filter and it is not a guarantee. The second is the limitations, which sit at the end of the discussion rather than in the abstract, and which are written by the authors about their own work. A paper with no limitations section is not a stronger paper. It is a paper that has decided not to tell you where it is weak, and that is the first thing an experienced reader goes looking for.

listenings.text: The mistake I made in my first year, and I watch new students make it every single semester, was reading a paper the way I read a chapter of a book. Word one to word ten thousand, in order, with a dictionary open. It took me an entire afternoon to get through one paper and by the end I could not have told you what the study actually found. So somebody in my lab sat me down and gave me an order that sounded almost rude. Read the last sentence of the background, then read the results, then stop. If those two do not interest you, close the tab. You have lost ninety seconds instead of four hours. And if they do interest you, then go back and read the method properly, because that is where you find out whether you believe the results at all. It felt wrong for about two weeks and then it felt obvious. Now I probably open thirty abstracts a week and I read maybe two papers properly, and that ratio is not laziness. That is the job.

Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the journal club. Before we start, three quick things about how this session runs, because we have several new people today. First, the paper was circulated on Monday and it is assumed that everybody has read at least the abstract and the figures. You are not expected to have read the entire discussion. Second, we go section by section, and the rule is that we talk about the method before we talk about the results. Every year somebody wants to argue about the conclusions in the first five minutes, and every year that conversation goes nowhere, because you cannot judge a finding until you know how it was measured. Third, and this is the one people find uncomfortable at first: anybody may say that they did not understand a section. Nobody here has read everything, and the person who admits that the baseline was not clear to them is usually the person who has spotted a real problem with the paper. We finish at half past four.
